newsitem.title: USA: Choose your value funds with care.
newsitem.headline: Choose your value funds with care.

text.p: The stock market's enormous gains during the past two years have been good news for fund shareholders. But their profits have varied, depending on what types of funds they held.

Most analysts divide stock funds into two broad categories. The first category includes growth-oriented funds, which have delivered strong gains during the past three years, posting 15.7 percent annual returns.
Such funds are willing to pay premium prices for shares of companies with strong earnings growth prospects. An example is rapidly growing software giant Microsoft Corp.
After adjusting for stock splits, Microsoft has climbed from about $30 in February 1995 to $98.375 on Thursday.

Value-oriented funds -- the second category -- take a different approach, investing in neglected shares of companies whose earnings prospects may appear uncertain. Value investors are less willing to pay premium prices for shares of popular companies.

Instead, they prefer to invest in stocks of firms whose value is unclear to most observers. Often, they'll buy a company's stock when the share price declines due to disappointing earnings. They may believe the firm has hidden assets or earnings potential, which will eventually attract Wall Street's attention.

One nice thing about value funds is that they tend to reduce risk in a portfolio. After all, the prices of the stocks they buy already reflect bad news about a company; thus, they have less distance to fall in the event of further setbacks.

By contrast, the popular stocks that growth funds hold generally suffer sharp declines when the firms that issue them fail to meet investors' often-high expectations. For example, even a minor sign of a decline in profit growth at companies such as Microsoft could cause their high-flying shares -- and the funds that hold them -- to plummet.

A recent study by the No-Load Fund analyst, a newsletter in Orinda, Calif., found that the worst one-year return for value funds during rolling 12-month periods from January 1976 through June 1996 has been a 15.4 percent loss, compared with a 20 percent loss for growth funds.

If you're worried that the stock market may be due for a setback, it might make sense to add a value fund or two to your portfolio to smooth the ride ahead. But choosing that fund requires considerable care.

The No-Load Fund Analyst also found that many so-called value funds don't have the courage of their convictions. That is, they often avoid the most battered stocks, which sometimes provide the biggest gains.
"Not just any old value manager will do," concludes the study. "The good ones are tough contrarians who have the guts to buy really cheap stuff and wait for value to be realised."
Fortunately, the newsletter's editors go on to identify some of the best value funds.

Their choices include funds such as Crabbe Huson Equity (800-541-9732; $2,000 minimum investment; no-load); Babson Value (800-422-2766; $1,000 minimum investment; no-load); Gabelli Asset (800-422-3554; $1,000 minimum investment; no-load); and T. Rowe Price Equity Income (800-638-5660; $2,500 minimum investment; no-load).
One especially solid pick is Oak Value (800-622-2474; $2,500 minimum investment; no-load), whose managers are followers of famous value investor Warren Buffett.

Their strategy is to invest in shares of companies with well-recognised products and strong market niches whose businesses offer the potential for strong cash flow. Equally important, they buy those firms' shares when they are trading at a discount from the firm's intrinsic value, based on assets and earnings potential.
Like many value investors, Oak Value's management team spends a great deal of time analysing specific companies rather than trying to bet on broad industry or economic trends.

They visit more than 100 companies each year, checking up on current holdings and looking for new ones. They concentrate their bets on a limited number of companies -- recently, around 25. That approach adds to the fund's risk. But it also means that the managers don't water down their best picks with others that aren't as solid.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers mutual funds for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
